title: Recovery incarnation continuity across a crash: re-mint and prove succession
description:
Objective: let a restore that was interrupted mid-flight establish a NEW recovery incarnation after restart and prove, durably, that it succeeds the interrupted one. Created by governor-f70d1157 at 14:52Z. A governor created this task; an ARCHITECT must plan it. What follows is measurement and constraint, not a plan.

WHY THIS EXISTS. architect-5b5302ee's planning audit of task-b6e3dd2a (Crash-safe two-slot recovery anchor installer) found that a PREPARED crash resume cannot reuse the incarnation it started with. That task is now BACKLOG and stays there until this lands. It is the only thing blocking it.

READ THE CONTRACT BEFORE PLANNING. apps/daemon/src/recovery/recovery-incarnation-contract.ts. Governor read it at 14:51Z and the design intent it encodes CHANGES THE OBVIOUS ANSWER:

- `RecoveryIncarnationKeyHandle = object` (line 42), and the doc comment above it says the adapter is the only thing that can map a handle back to key material, "through a module-private WeakMap. A fabricated or structurally cloned object is a different identity and resolves to nothing."
- `RecoveryIncarnationMinted.keyHandle` carries the comment: "Non-enumerable, so it cannot ride along in serialized evidence."

SO THE EPHEMERAL PRIVATE KEY IS A DELIBERATE SECURITY PROPERTY, NOT AN OVERSIGHT. Do not "fix" it by making the handle serializable or the key extractable. That would defeat a property the author built on purpose, and it is almost certainly the wrong task.

WHAT IS ALREADY DURABLE, and this is the material to build on: RecoveryIncarnationBinding is fully serializable and carries incarnationRef, keyEpochRef, incarnationDigest, verificationKeyFingerprint, publicKeyAlgorithm ("Ed25519"), publicKeySpkiHex, bindingDigest, and a RecoveryIncarnationProof of {challengeDigest, signatureHex, verified}. A prior incarnation is therefore fully IDENTIFIABLE and its signatures remain VERIFIABLE after a crash, even though it can no longer SIGN.

THE SHAPE THIS TASK SHOULD TAKE, subject to the architect's judgement: on resume, mint a FRESH incarnation and record a durable succession record binding the new incarnationRef/keyEpochRef to the interrupted one's, so the chain from the original restore command is provable end to end. The exact succession record, where it is persisted, and how it is verified are the design decisions to make and to justify in planningNotes.

CONSTRAINTS THAT ARE NOT NEGOTIABLE:
- Do not make the private key durable, extractable, or serializable.
- A succession record must not let a caller claim succession from an incarnation it cannot prove it held. Fail closed with a stable reason code and the refusing layer per epic rail 6; a forged or unverifiable predecessor reference is REFUSED, never UNKNOWN-and-admitted.
- This composes @moe/store and the existing crypto port; it does not invent a second key lifecycle.
- Per Clause 1, name task-b6e3dd2a as the consumer and record its id in the plan.

NOT IN SCOPE: changing task-684e6972's minting behaviour (it is DONE and QA-approved against its own scope, and this is a follow-on, not a fix); the two-slot anchor installer itself (that is task-b6e3dd2a); backup generation (task-5606947a, DONE).

Hard dependencies: none. task-684e6972 and task-5606947a are both DONE with published root exports — RecoveryIncarnation* at apps/daemon/src/index.ts and createBackupGeneration/verifyBackupGeneration at packages/store/src/index.ts.

Verification: pnpm --filter @moe/daemon typecheck && pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test, plus whatever store-level leg the design requires.

Size: if the plan exceeds 12 steps or 10 distinct affectedFiles, SPLIT it and say so rather than padding.
definitionOfDone: A durable succession record exists that binds a freshly minted recovery incarnation to the interrupted predecessor it succeeds, carrying at minimum both incarnationRefs and both keyEpochRefs, and it survives process restart — proven by writing it, reopening the store in a separate step, and reading it back rather than by asserting against an in-memory value.

Succession is PROVEN, not asserted: the new incarnation's claim to succeed the predecessor is verified against the predecessor's durable binding (verificationKeyFingerprint / publicKeySpkiHex / bindingDigest), so a caller that never held the predecessor cannot manufacture the link. A forged or unverifiable predecessor reference is REFUSED with its stable code and refusing layer, never admitted as UNKNOWN.

The private key remains ephemeral. A test asserts the succession record and every durable artifact contain NO key material and no serialized key handle — asserted by inspecting the persisted bytes, not by trusting non-enumerability, since the point is what survives serialization.

Every refusal path asserts the exact stable reason code AND the refusing layer per epic rail 6, and the case sweep asserts it generated a non-zero number of cases so an emptied sweep cannot pass silently.

The full chain from the original restore command to the current incarnation is reconstructible from durable records alone after a restart — demonstrated over at least two successive crashes, not one, so a scheme that only handles a single hop fails.

implementationPlan.description: TDD red: write apps/daemon/src/recovery/recovery-succession.test.ts against the not-yet-existing service. The spliced-proof case is built so ONLY the recomputation catches it: `bindingDigest` is altered and the proof is left untouched, so `port.verify` still returns true under the binding's own key and only `digestOf("challenge", bindingDigest) === proof.challengeDigest` can refuse it.

implementationPlan.description: Implement predecessor verification in apps/daemon/src/recovery/recovery-succession.ts (first half): given a candidate predecessor incarnationRef, load its durable RecoveryIncarnationBinding from the store and prove it is genuine before anything else happens. Three checks, in this order, all failing closed: (1) the binding exists on its aggregate -> else RECOVERY_PREDECESSOR_NOT_FOUND; (2) recomputed digestOf("challenge", binding.bindingDigest) equals binding.proof.challengeDigest -> else RECOVERY_PREDECESSOR_UNVERIFIABLE, which is what stops a valid proof lifted from a different binding; (3) port.verify(Buffer.from(binding.publicKeySpkiHex,"hex"), Buffer.from(binding.proof.challengeDigest,"hex"), Buffer.from(binding.proof.signatureHex,"hex")) returns exactly true -> else RECOVERY_PREDECESSOR_UNVERIFIABLE. Compare with `!== true` rather than falsiness, matching recovery-incarnation.ts:118-121, so a port returning a truthy non-boolean never authorizes. Wrap every port call in the exported attemptPort helper so a throwing port maps to a fixed refusal and no provider message reaches evidence. Also verify binding.verificationKeyFingerprint equals digestOf("key", spkiBytes) recomputed from publicKeySpkiHex, so a binding whose fingerprint does not cover its own published key is refused. This step deliberately reads ONLY durable fields: the predecessor's private key is gone by design and must not be needed.
implementationPlan.note:
PART ONE — the durable anchor. `recovery-incarnation-anchor.ts` (217 lines) + byte-exact `.js` bridge (`export * from "./recovery-incarnation-anchor.ts";`, LF, no BOM, confirmed with `od -c` against the existing recovery-incarnation.js shape). Exports exactly two functions.

`anchorIncarnation(store, request, binding) -> boolean` commits under commandKind "recovery.incarnate", targetAggregateId `recovery-incarnation:${incarnationRef}`, expectedVersion 0. NO try/catch anywhere: the version conflict is RETURNED by the store as a NO_BUSINESS_EFFECT decision, so it is read off `response.decision.effectDisposition`, and a genuine store fault keeps throwing instead of being reported as a benign duplicate. Bytes are produced by a canonical serializer that writes ONE fixed field order rather than the caller's key order, so a re-anchor after a crash is recognisable as a repeat — re-anchoring a byte-identical binding returns true (idempotent), which is what makes a crash between anchoring and recording the succession recoverable by simply retrying.

`readAnchoredIncarnation(store, projectId, ref)` pages readCommandDecisionsAfter filtering projectId + commandKind + EFFECTS_COMMITTED + targetAggregateId, then runs a BOUNDED EXACT-SHAPE decode: exact key sets for both the binding (11) and its proof (3), hex64 on all six digest fields, bounded hex on the signature and SPKI (Ed25519 signatures are 128 hex chars, so HEX64 there would have rejected every real row), pinned publicKeyAlgorithm and schemaVersion. A drifted, truncated or extra-field row decodes to null and reads as ABSENT rather than being admitted with fields the reader would be free to invent. The aggregate id is then RECOMPUTED from the decoded content, so a row filed under one incarnation while carrying another's binding is dropped.

CONTRACT — added the sixth stable code RECOVERY_INCARNATION_ANCHOR_UNAVAILABLE and its fixed refusal constant; the five existing codes and their five refusal constants are byte-identical. Also added RECOVERY_INCARNATION_ANCHOR_COMMAND_KIND, the incarnation aggregate prefix/id helper, `RecoveryDurableWriteRequest`, `RecoverySuccessionRequest`, and `snapshotSuccessionRequest` — a descriptor-based exact-7-key reader modelled on the incarnation contract's `snapshotRequest`: one synchronous read of own property DESCRIPTORS before any await (so an accessor or proxy cannot answer differently the second time), extra keys refused rather than dropped, and both refs bounded to hex64 so a caller-chosen prefix or separator cannot steer the aggregate id it becomes. Contract is 241 lines — under the cap but with little headroom, so the service stays self-contained rather than pushing more shapes here.

PART TWO — `verifyAnchoredPredecessor` in recovery-succession.ts. Four checks, all failing closed: (1) `readAnchoredIncarnation` returns non-null else RECOVERY_PREDECESSOR_NOT_FOUND — a minted-but-unanchored binding is indistinguishable from one a caller minted a moment ago to claim succession from, which is exactly the forgery the anchor exists to defeat; (2) recomputed `digestOf("challenge", bindingDigest) === proof.challengeDigest`, placed BEFORE the signature check because a proof lifted from another genuine binding verifies perfectly in isolation and only this recomputation catches it; (3) recomputed `digestOf("key", spkiBytes) === verificationKeyFingerprint`, so a binding naming one epoch's fingerprint while carrying another's public key is refused even though the signature would still pass against the key that is really there; (4) `port.verify(...) !== true`, matching recovery-incarnation.ts:118-123 so a truthy non-boolean never authorizes. The port call is wrapped in the exported `attemptPort`, so a throwing port maps to a fixed refusal and no provider message reaches evidence.

Reads ONLY durable public fields; the predecessor's private key is never needed.

The only remaining errors are the expected mid-TDD ones — recovery-succession.ts does not yet export `createRecoverySuccessionService`/`readSuccessionChain` (steps 5 and 6). implementationPlan.description: Implement minting and the succession proof in recovery-succession.ts (second half). Compose the EXISTING createRecoveryIncarnationService to mint the successor -- do not open a second key lifecycle (task rail 4). Build successionDigest = digestOf("succession", predecessorIncarnationRef, predecessorKeyEpochRef, predecessorBindingDigest, successorIncarnationRef, successorKeyEpochRef, successorBindingDigest); digestOf is already domain-separated and length-framed, which is why the multi-part input is safe. Derive the succession challenge as digestOf("succession-challenge", successionDigest), sign its hex-decoded RAW bytes with the SUCCESSOR's in-memory key handle via port.sign, and self-verify through port.verify with `!== true` before publishing, exactly as the mint service does. A sign or verify failure is RECOVERY_SUCCESSION_PROOF_UNAVAILABLE. The successor signs; the predecessor cannot and is never asked to. Assemble the frozen RecoverySuccessionRecord. Then call port.destroy on any handle this module obtained but is not returning, so a failure path does not leave key material alive longer than a success path would.
implementationPlan.note:
Minting and the succession proof landed in recovery-succession.ts (now 170 lines).

`mintSuccessor` composes the EXISTING `createRecoveryIncarnationService(port)` — no second key lifecycle, per task rail 4. A mint refusal is mapped to RECOVERY_SUCCESSION_PROOF_UNAVAILABLE rather than echoed: the incarnation service's codes belong to the RECOVERY_INCARNATION layer, and passing one through would report a foreign layer's vocabulary from this one, which is exactly the refusal-code drift epic rail 6 exists to stop. Semantically it is also true — a successor that could not be minted leaves this layer with no proof to offer.

`proveSuccession` builds successionDigest = digestOf("succession", predIncarnationRef, predKeyEpochRef, predBindingDigest, succIncarnationRef, succKeyEpochRef, succBindingDigest). Six parts in one call is safe only because `digestOf` is domain-separated AND length-framed — without the framing a caller able to steer one ref could slide the boundary between two parts onto another statement's digest. Then challengeDigest = digestOf("succession-challenge", successionDigest), and the SUCCESSOR signs `Buffer.from(challengeDigest, "hex")` — the RAW 32 bytes, never the hex text, matching recovery-incarnation.ts:108-109. The signature is COPIED with `Uint8Array.from` before verification for the same reason the mint copies its SPKI: the bytes that get verified must be the bytes that get published while the port still holds a reference. Self-verified through `port.verify` with `!== true`, so a truthy non-boolean cannot pass. Sign or verify failure -> RECOVERY_SUCCESSION_PROOF_UNAVAILABLE. Both port calls go through `attemptPort`, so a throwing provider maps to a fixed refusal with no diagnostic reaching evidence.

The predecessor is never asked to sign — its key died with its process. That asymmetry is the whole design, and it is why a crashed incarnation can still be succeeded.

`record.restoreCommandId` is read from the MINTED binding, not echoed from the request, so the record names the command the successor was actually minted for rather than whatever the caller typed.

`discardHandle` wraps `port.destroy` in a try/catch that swallows only the cleanup failure, matching the mint service's `discard`: a cleanup error must never replace the primary result it was cleaning up after. The service returns no key handle, so step 6 calls this on every path — success and failure alike — and no failure path leaves key material alive longer than a success path would.

implementationPlan.description: Implement durable single-shot persistence and the chain walk in recovery-succession.ts, and add its byte-exact .js bridge. The aggregate keyed on the PREDECESSOR plus expectedVersion 0 is the single-shot enforcement: the store itself refuses a second succession from the same predecessor, so the chain cannot fork and two callers cannot both claim to succeed one incarnation. Map the resulting version conflict to RECOVERY_SUCCESSION_ALREADY_RECORDED -- catch that specific conflict, never a bare catch-all that would also swallow a real store fault and report a benign duplicate. Add readSuccessionChain(store, projectId, fromIncarnationRef) that pages readCommandDecisionsAfter, filters exactly as restart-reconciliation does, indexes records by successorIncarnationRef and walks predecessor links backwards to the origin, returning the ordered chain plus the originating restoreCommandId. Confirm each production source is <=250 physical lines with `grep -c ''` (PowerShell Measure-Object -Line undercounts by skipping blank lines); move shapes into the contract file if the service is over.

ANCHOR BEFORE SUCCEED, with the crash argument in a comment at the service factory. A crash between the two writes leaves an anchored incarnation with no succession record, which is recoverable — the next run mints a new successor and retries. The reverse order would leave a succession record pointing at an incarnation that was never anchored: a dangling reference the predecessor check refuses forever, with no repair path. Anchor failure returns RECOVERY_INCARNATION_ANCHOR_UNAVAILABLE and writes no succession record.

A REAL DEFECT THE TESTS CAUGHT, worth reading before review. My first commit used commandId `recovery-succeed:${predecessorIncarnationRef}` — predecessor only, mirroring the aggregate. The rival-successor test then failed with a THROWN `IdempotencyConflictError: the scoped command ID was reused for a different request` out of decision-ledger-replay.ts:29, never reaching the expected-version check. The ledger validates the idempotency key BEFORE expected-version, so a predecessor-only command id converts the conflict this layer is supposed to MAP into an exception that escapes it. Fixed by naming both ends in the command id (`recovery-succeed:<pred>:<succ>`) while the aggregate still names only the predecessor: a rival successor now gets a distinct id and receives the returned version conflict -> RECOVERY_SUCCESSION_ALREADY_RECORDED, and a byte-identical retry still replays cleanly under its own id. The reason is recorded as a comment at the call site, because the ordering it depends on is not visible from this file.

NO try/catch on either durable write. Both conflicts are RETURNED as NO_BUSINESS_EFFECT decisions and are read off `effectDisposition`; a genuine store fault keeps throwing rather than being reported as a benign duplicate.

`readSuccessionChain` refuses up front if the starting ref is not anchored (RECOVERY_PREDECESSOR_NOT_FOUND), indexes records by successorIncarnationRef, and walks predecessor links backwards. Rows whose targetAggregateId does not match `successionAggregateId(record.predecessorIncarnationRef)` recomputed from DECODED content are dropped, so a row filed under one predecessor while naming another cannot be walked. The visited set refuses a repeat with RECOVERY_SUCCESSION_ALREADY_RECORDED rather than looping: the single-shot write makes a cycle unreachable today, but a read path that trusts a write invariant it does not itself enforce is one bad row away from hanging the daemon at startup. The originating restoreCommandId is read from the ANCHORED ORIGIN BINDING, never from the newest record — reachable precisely because every incarnation is anchored as it is minted.

The successor's key handle is destroyed in a `finally`, so every path — anchor failure, proof failure, conflict, success — releases it identically.

Implement durable persistence and the chain walk in recovery-succession.ts, and add its byte-exact .js bridge. Order matters and is part of the correctness argument.

FIRST anchor the successor: call anchorIncarnation from recovery-incarnation-anchor.ts on the freshly minted successor binding, so it becomes a durable incarnation in its own right. This is what makes the chain survive more than one hop -- an unanchored successor is an unanchored PREDECESSOR after the next crash, and the second hop would then fail RECOVERY_PREDECESSOR_NOT_FOUND. An anchor failure refuses with RECOVERY_INCARNATION_ANCHOR_UNAVAILABLE and no succession record is written.

THEN record the succession via store.commitExpectedVersionDecision following the restart-reconciliation.ts pattern, with targetAggregateId = `recovery-succession:${predecessorIncarnationRef}` and expectedVersion: 0. Keying that aggregate on the PREDECESSOR with expectedVersion 0 is the single-shot enforcement: the store itself refuses a second succession from the same predecessor, so the chain cannot fork and two callers cannot both claim to succeed one incarnation. Map that specific version conflict to RECOVERY_SUCCESSION_ALREADY_RECORDED -- catch that conflict precisely, never a bare catch-all that would also swallow a real store fault and report a benign duplicate.

Anchor-before-succeed is the safe crash order, and say so in a comment. A crash between the two writes leaves an anchored incarnation with no succession record, which is recoverable -- the next run simply retries the succession. The reverse order would leave a succession record pointing at an incarnation that was never anchored, which is an unrecoverable dangling reference that the predecessor check would reject forever.

Then add readSuccessionChain(store, projectId, fromIncarnationRef): page readCommandDecisionsAfter, filter exactly as restart-reconciliation does, index succession records by successorIncarnationRef and walk predecessor links backwards to the origin, returning the ordered chain plus the originating restoreCommandId read from the ANCHORED origin binding -- which is reachable precisely because every incarnation is anchored. Bound the walk with a visited set and refuse on a repeat rather than looping forever: the single-shot write makes a cycle unreachable today, but a read path that trusts a write invariant it does not itself enforce is one bad row away from hanging the daemon at startup. planningNotes.approachesConsidered:
THE HONEST LIMIT OF WHAT SUCCESSION CAN PROVE -- READ THIS BEFORE REVIEWING DoD 2.

DoD 2 says a caller that never held the predecessor cannot manufacture the link. Taken literally as a cryptographic possession proof, that is IMPOSSIBLE under this design, and deliberately so: the predecessor's private key is destroyed at crash, so it can never sign an attestation naming its successor, and everything it left behind is durable and therefore readable by anyone who can read the store. No scheme recovers possession proof from an intentionally ephemeral key. The only way to get one would be to make the key durable, which task rail 2 forbids outright and which would defeat the property the contract author built on purpose.

So I did NOT weaken the key lifecycle, and I did not narrow the DoD either. The design supplies the strongest guarantee actually available, which is what the DoD's own wording asks for -- it names the durable fields (verificationKeyFingerprint / publicKeySpkiHex / bindingDigest) as the verification inputs, so store-authorized succession is what it already describes. Concretely, three independent gates:
1. EXISTENCE: the predecessor's binding must be durably present on its aggregate. A fabricated ref refuses with RECOVERY_PREDECESSOR_NOT_FOUND.
2. SELF-PROOF: the predecessor's own signature must verify against its own published SPKI, AND its proof.challengeDigest must equal a recomputed digestOf("challenge", bindingDigest), AND its verificationKeyFingerprint must equal a recomputed digestOf("key", spki). The recomputation is what makes this more than a signature check: a proof lifted from a DIFFERENT genuine binding verifies perfectly in isolation and is caught only by recomputing the challenge from this binding.
3. SINGLE-SHOT: the succession aggregate is keyed on the PREDECESSOR's incarnationRef and written with expectedVersion 0, so the store itself refuses a second succession from the same predecessor. The chain cannot fork and two callers cannot both claim one incarnation.

WHAT REMAINS TRUE AND SHOULD BE SAID PLAINLY TO QA AND TO ANY SECURITY REVIEWER: an actor with write access to the durable store can assert a succession. Store write authority IS the trust boundary here; this task does not and cannot create a second one. That is a property of the ephemeral-key design, not a defect introduced by this task, and it should be recorded rather than papered over.

AGGREGATE KEYED ON THE PREDECESSOR, NOT THE SUCCESSOR. Rejected: keying on the successor's incarnationRef. The successor is freshly minted and unique per attempt, so expectedVersion 0 on it is trivially satisfied every time and enforces nothing. Keying on the predecessor is what makes fork prevention real.

RECOMPUTE THE CHALLENGE, DO NOT JUST VERIFY THE SIGNATURE. Rejected: verifying proof.signatureHex against publicKeySpkiHex over proof.challengeDigest alone. That accepts a proof spliced from any other genuine binding by the same key epoch. Recomputing digestOf("challenge", bindingDigest) and comparing binds the proof to THIS binding. Drill (b) in step 8 exists to keep that check alive.

COMPOSE THE MINT SERVICE, DO NOT REIMPLEMENT IT. Rejected: minting the successor inside this module. Task rail 4 forbids a second key lifecycle, and a parallel minting path would drift from the reviewed one. The successor is minted by createRecoveryIncarnationService; this module only signs the succession statement with the successor's in-memory handle.

CONSUMER, per Clause 1: task-b6e3dd2a (Crash-safe two-slot recovery anchor installer). It is in BACKLOG and, per the description, blocked solely on this task -- its PREPARED crash resume cannot reuse the incarnation it started with, which is the defect this task closes.

planningNotes.risks:
1. THE SIGNED-BYTES DETAIL IS THE MOST LIKELY SILENT FAILURE. If the worker signs or verifies the hex STRING instead of the hex-decoded raw bytes, every predecessor verification fails and the symptom looks like a broken key or a bad port rather than an encoding mistake. recovery-incarnation.ts:108-121 is the reference; match it exactly.

2. A SPLICED PROOF VERIFIES. proof.signatureHex from a different genuine binding of the same key epoch passes a naive signature check. Only the recomputed digestOf("challenge", bindingDigest) equality catches it. Do not treat that check as redundant belt-and-braces; it is the actual guard.

3. THE ALREADY_RECORDED MAPPING MUST BE NARROW. Map the specific expected-version conflict to RECOVERY_SUCCESSION_ALREADY_RECORDED. A bare catch-all would also swallow a genuine store fault and report a benign duplicate, turning a real durability failure into a green path.

4. THE CHAIN WALK MUST BE BOUNDED INDEPENDENTLY. The single-shot write makes a cycle unreachable today, but a read path that trusts a write invariant it does not itself enforce hangs the daemon at startup on one bad row. Keep the visited set and refuse on a repeat.

5. DoD 3 IS ABOUT SERIALIZED BYTES, NOT TYPES. Assert over the JSON actually read back out of the reopened store. A non-enumerable property is invisible to JSON.stringify, so a type-level or in-memory assertion proves nothing about what survives -- and what survives is the entire question.

6. DoD 1 AND RAIL 5 REQUIRE A REAL REOPEN. Close the store and reopen it from the same file in a separate step. A test that reads back through the same live handle proves nothing crossed a durability boundary.

7. TWO HOPS, NOT ONE (DoD 5). A design that stores a single predecessor pointer per incarnation passes a one-crash test and fails the real requirement. The chain test must be A -> B -> C.

8. SURFACE COUNT. index-surface.test.ts pins the export count and asserts exact set equality. Adding exports without bumping the count and the list turns the suite red for a reason unrelated to this feature.

9. SHARED WORKING DIRECTORY. packages/store/package.json was already dirty from a foreign task at plan time, and restart-reconciliation.ts sits at exactly 250 lines adjacent to task-5855a9c6's in-flight continuation work. Do not edit restart-reconciliation.ts. Attribute any foreign red by path before treating it as this task's defect, and during the drills trust the red test over `git status`.

10. IF THE DESIGN EVER SEEMS TO NEED A DURABLE KEY, STOP. Task rail 2 makes that a product decision, not an implementation choice: report_blocked and say so rather than weakening the ephemeral-key property.
